claim: Acinetobacter baumannii bacteria recently emerged as global pathogens with nosocomial mortality rates reaching 19–54%.

claim: Acinetobacter gains antibiotic resistance remarkably rapidly.
source: Acinetobacter gains antibiotic resistance remarkably rapidly (Antunes et al., 2014; Joly Guillou, 2005)

claim: DNA released via cell lysis is readily available for HGT.

claim: DNA released via cell lysis may be partially protected from the environment.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations indicating gaps in knowledge.

claim: Contact-dependent killing by Acinetobacter can increase HGT rates from E. coli by up to 3 orders of magnitude.
source: In this paper, we showed that contact-dependent killing by Acinetobacter can increase HGT rates from E. coli by up to 3 orders of magnitude
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Killing by one strain in a spatially-structured community makes DNA available for uptake by nearby, non-killing cells.
source: Significantly, we also showed that killing by one strain in a spatially-structured community makes DNA available for uptake by nearby, non-killing cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: DNA uptake and transformation parameters fit using purified plasmid DNA accurately predicted HGT by DNA released in situ.
source: Interestingly, DNA uptake and transformation parameters fit using purified plasmid DNA accurately predicted HGT by DNA released in situ.
evidence: The claim is supported by model predictions matching experimental data (Figure 4).

claim: For contact-dependent killing, predation can occur only at the perimeter of micro-colonies, where there is contact between predator and prey cells.
source: For contact-dependent killing, predation can occur only at the perimeter of micro-colonies, where there is contact between predator and prey cells (Schwarz et al., 2010a; Borenstein et al., 2015; Hood et al., 2010; Schwarz et al., 2010b; MacIntyre et al., 2010; LeRoux et al., 2012) (see also Supplemental Videos 9–12).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and experimental observations in Videos 9-12.

claim: Using N* to represent perimeter cells yielded a slightly better optimal fit to the data than assuming all cells are equally vulnerable.
source: This use of N* to represent perimeter cells yielded a slightly better optimal fit to our data than assuming all cells are equally vulnerable, but the difference was not dramatic.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model fits with different assumptions.

claim: The difference between the total number of cells and the number of perimeter cells only becomes significant when the population has grown much greater than the initial cell number.
source: The difference between the total number of cells and the number of perimeter cells only becomes significant when the population has grown much greater than the initial cell number (compare solid blue to dashed orange lines in Figure 3—figure supplement 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by model analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The model can be modified for the case when killing is mediated by diffusible molecules by simply replacing N* with N.
source: The model presented here can be modified for the case when killing is mediated by diffusible molecules, where there is no distinction between interior and exterior cells in a micro-colony, by simply replacing N* with N.
evidence: The claim is a statement about model flexibility based on reasoning.

claim: Killing is most important for HGT when the prey is at low density, the predator is at high density, and the interaction time is short.
source: Our model revealed that killing is most important for HGT when the prey is at low density, the predator is at high density, and the interaction time is short (Figure 5c,f), which was confirmed by experimental data (Figure 7a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by model predictions and experimental validation.

claim: Killing is less important for HGT when the prey outnumbers the predator, because enough prey DNA is released by spontaneous lysis.
source: Killing is less important for HGT when the prey outnumbers the predator, because enough prey DNA is released by spontaneous lysis that the additional DNA released by killing no longer provides much advantage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from model results and reasoning about DNA availability.

claim: Killing provides less HGT enhancement when the interaction time is longer, because killing Acinetobacter deplete their donor DNA source by killing neighboring prey E. coli.
source: Similarly, killing provides less HGT enhancement when the interaction time is longer, because killing Acinetobacter deplete their donor DNA source by killing neighboring prey E. coli, whereas the non-killing mutants have a slower, but exponentially growing, source of DNA from spontaneously lysing E. coli.
evidence: The claim is inferred from model results and reasoning about population dynamics.

claim: The seeding ratio at which contact-dependent killing most enhances HGT is the same condition in which it provides the strongest competitive advantage in terms of cell growth.
source: Interestingly, this seeding ratio at which contact-dependent killing most enhances HGT - when the predator outnumbers the prey - is the same condition in which it provides the strongest competitive advantage in terms of cell growth (Borenstein et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published work (Borenstein et al. 2015).

claim: High predator cell density is the condition that induces fratricide-mediated HGT in Streptococci.
source: High predator cell density is also the condition that induces fratricide-mediated HGT in Streptococci (Steinmoen et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Steinmoen et al. 2002.

claim: High predator cell density simultaneously induces both T6SS expression and competence in V. cholerae.
source: and simultaneously induces both T6SS expression and competence in V. cholera (Borgeaud et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Borgeaud et al. 2015.

claim: T6SS regulation does not always depend on high cell density, and it can be quite complex and varied, even within strains of the same species.
source: However, T6SS regulation does not always depend on high cell density, and it can be quite complex and varied, even within strains of the same species, likely reflecting the wide range of ecological contexts and functions performed by the T6SS (Miyata et al., 2013; Bernard et al., 2010; Weber et al., 2013; Weber et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple sources.

claim: The only demonstrated advantages of T6SS are at high cell density.
source: Given that the only demonstrated advantages are at high cell density, it remains an open question what, if any, selective advantages the T6SS may provide at lower cell density.
evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the current state of knowledge.

claim: T6SS regulation in A. baylyi has not been extensively characterized with respect to cell density.
source: While T6SS regulation in A. baylyi has not been extensively characterized with respect to cell density (Weber et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Weber et al. 2016.

claim: T6SS in A. baylyi is active and functional in standard in vitro conditions.
source: it is active and functional in standard in vitro conditions (Weber et al., 2013; Basler et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Weber et al. 2013 and Basler et al. 2013.

claim: T6SS-mediated killing of E. coli was observed at all times in the Supplemental Videos 1–6.
source: and we observed T6SS-mediated killing of E. coli at all times in the Supplemental Videos 1–6.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations in Videos 1-6.

claim: Neither DNase nor competing DNA would eliminate the HGT enhancement provided by killing.
source: Although our model predicted neither condition would eliminated the HGT enhancement provided by killing in our model, both strategies were predicted to reduce HGT when at realistic levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by model predictions shown in Figure 6.

claim: DNA degradation began to reduce HGT when DNA half life was less than 2–3 min, which is just longer than the half life of free DNA in saliva.
source: DNA degradation began to reduce HGT when DNA half life was less than 2–3 min (Figure 6a), which is just longer than the half life of free DNA in saliva, about 1 min (Mercer et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by model predictions and comparison to published data.

claim: Competing DNA began to reduce HGT at about 10^9 kb or greater, which would be 10–100 kb of extracellular DNA per cell at carrying capacity.
source: Competing DNA began to reduce HGT at about 109 kb or greater (Figure 6e), and given that our agar spots could support 107–108 cells, that would be 10–100 kb of extracellular DNA per cell at carrying capacity.
evidence: The claim is supported by model predictions and calculation.

claim: DNase can reduce HGT to wild type Acinetobacter by nearly 10^4-fold even at high seeding densities.
source: Our experimental results supported this, showing that DNase can reduce HGT to wild type Acinetobacter by nearly 104-fold even at high seeding densities
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The reduced efficacy of competing DNA at high cell density is likely because the high initial killing rate releases a large amount of prey DNA at once, overcoming competitive inhibition.
source: The reduced efficacy of competing DNA in this condition is likely because the high initial killing rate releases a large amount of prey DNA at once, overcoming competitive inhibition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental observations and reasoning about DNA dynamics.

claim: Competing DNA was nearly 10-fold less effective than predicted.
source: Interestingly, competing DNA was nearly 10-fold less effective than predicted
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental data to model predictions.

claim: The reduced efficacy of competing DNA may reflect its physical exclusion from dense microbial communities.
source: which may reflect its physical exclusion from dense microbial communities
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about experimental observations.

claim: There appears to be a small sub-population of Acinetobacter with access to prey cell DNA protected from DNase.
source: The potential importance of non-isotropic DNA concentration is also suggested by the observation that there appears to be a small sub-population of Acinetobacter with access to prey cell DNA protected from DNase (Figure 7e)
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental observations shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Contact-dependent killing appears to provide a sub-population of cells with privileged access to DNA that is protected from DNase.
source: Additionally, the observation that contact-dependent killing appears to provide a sub-population of cells with privileged access to DNA that is protected from DNase may help explain how HGT can occur so frequently in real-world environments where DNA is quickly degraded.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental observations and reasoning about environmental HGT.

claim: A. baylyi and A. baumannii are closely enough related that they are difficult to distinguish with standard phenotypic tests used in the clinic.
source: While we used A. baylyi as a model for the more clinically threatening A. baumannii, the two are closely enough related that they are difficult to distinguish with standard phenotypic tests used in the clinic (Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chen et al. 2007.

claim: A. baylyi can opportunistically infect humans, including case clusters in hospitals.
source: Indeed, careful re-examination of clinical isolates recently revealed that A. baylyi can also opportunistically infect humans, including case clusters in hospitals (Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chen et al. 2008.

claim: A clinical A. baylyi isolate contained the first blaSIM-1 carbapenemase reported in China.
source: It was a clinical A. baylyi isolate that contained the first blaSIM-1 carbapenemase reported in China (Zhou et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhou et al. 2011.

claim: A. baylyi may be causing additional infections that are either misidentified as A. baumannii or identified nonspecifically as Acinetobacter.
source: and the difficulty of distinguishing between the two suggests that A. baylyi may in fact be causing additional infections that are either misidentified as A. baumannii or identified nonspecifically as Acinetobacter (Chen et al., 2007, 2008).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the difficulty of distinguishing the species.

claim: A. baylyi may serve as an easily sampled reservoir of genetic diversity for A. baumannii.
source: Perhaps more importantly, A. baylyi may serve as an easily sampled reservoir of genetic diversity for A. baumannii, due to the extremely high transformability of A. baylyi coupled to the ease with which Acinetobacter species exchange DNA.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the characteristics of A. baylyi.

claim: The carbapenemase gene blaOXA23 has been found in multiple Acinetobacter species isolated from both humans and animals, including both A. baumannii and A. baylyi.
source: For example, another carbapenemase gene, blaOXA23, has been found in multiple Acinetobacter species isolated from both humans and animals, including both A. baumannii and A. baylyi (Smet et al., 2012; Nigro and Hall, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Smet et al. 2012 and Nigro and Hall 2016.

claim: The population dynamics revealed in this work are likely important in the microbiome and microbial evolution more broadly.
source: In addition to helping to explain, predict, and combat the rapid spread of multi drug-resistance, particularly among Acinetobacter, the population dynamics revealed here are likely important in the microbiome and microbial evolution more broadly.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the widespread distribution of relevant mechanisms.

claim: Both the T6SS and natural competence are widespread among gram-negative bacteria.
source: Both the T6SS (Schwarz et al., 2010a) and natural competence (Johnsborg et al., 2007) are widespread among gram-negative bacteria
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schwarz et al. 2010a and Johnsborg et al. 2007.

claim: Both competence and other neighbor killing mechanisms are found in both gram-negatives and gram-positives.
source: and both competence and other neighbor killing mechanisms are found in both gram-negatives and gram-positives.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge from the field.

claim: The results are likely broadly generalizable and may contribute to understanding the known increase of HGT within biofilms.
source: Therefore, our results are likely broadly generalizable and may contribute to understanding the known increase of HGT within biofilms (Madsen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the widespread distribution of relevant mechanisms and citation to Madsen et al. 2012.

claim: The method presented for quantifying natural competence with standardized parameters may help researchers address other outstanding questions about microbial evolution.
source: The method presented here for quantifying natural competence with standardized parameters may also help researchers address other outstanding questions about microbial evolution (Vos et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential future applications, with citation to Vos et al. 2015.
